name: Rebkong Amdo Tibetan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 12 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Caplow, Nancy J. 2016. Reconstructing stress in Proto-Tibetan: Evidence from Balti and Rebkong Amdo. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 39(2): 180-221. DOI 10.1075/ltba.39.2.01cap. Supporting: Caplow, Nancy J. 2016. Stress patterns and acoustic correlates of stress in Balti Tibetan. Himalayan Linguistics 15(2): 1-49 (eScholarship qt0k86k32k); Tournadre, Nicolas & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2023. The Tibetic Languages. Villejuif: LACITO, sec. 7.3.3; Lim, Keh Sheng. 2018. The Tonal and Intonational Phonology of Lhasa Tibetan. PhD dissertation, University of Ottawa, sec. 1.3.3.1.
catalog_locator: Caplow 2016 LTBA 39(2): author's abstract, p. 180, on the open publisher page (jbe-platform.com); body pp. 180-221 paywalled, not opened. Supporting: Caplow 2016 HL 15(2) abstract p. 1 and fn. 3 p. 2; Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 7.3.3 pp. 241-242; Lim 2018 sec. 1.3.3.1 pp. 24-25.
catalog_quote: This paper offers a synchronic description of stress patterns in two conservative varieties of Tibetan, and a diachronic reconstruction of stress patterns in Proto-Tibetan. For both Balti and Rebkong Amdo, stress falls on the second syllable (σ2) of disyllabic non-verbs — nouns, adjectives, and numerals. ... Disyllabic verbs are never stressed on σ2. For Balti, robust evidence shows that they are stressed on the first syllable (σ1). Limited data for Rebkong Amdo suggests the same pattern. Thus σ1 stress is tentatively reconstructed for verbs in Proto-Tibetan.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Amdo Tibetan is not in the catalog. the list of works with stress in the title holds one item, Caplow's 2009 UCSB dissertation (607 pp.) on stress and Tibetan tonogenesis, which uses Rebkong Amdo as one of its two atonal source varieties; it is ProQuest-restricted (record opened, no abstract, no free copy; UCSB ADRL has no record; The author's follow-up, Caplow 2016 LTBA 39(2) 'Reconstructing stress in Proto-Tibetan: Evidence from Balti and Rebkong Amdo' (not in the list of works with stress in the title), gives the same data in a published form; only its abstract was reachable (paywalled at John Benjamins, OpenAlex closed), saved with the page HTML and OpenAlex record under with. That abstract is the best first-hand statement obtained: Rebkong Amdo disyllabic nouns/adjectives/numerals carry stress on the second (final) syllable; disyllabic verbs are never σ2-stressed and on limited data are σ1-stressed. On-disk secondary sources agree (Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 7.3.3, 9.5.6; Lim 2018 sec. 1.3.3.1; Caplow 2016 HL Balti paper fn. 3 gives Rebkong Amdo [xso.'ra] 'sickle'). Recommended acquisition: the 2016 LTBA full text (pp. 180-221) first, then the 2009 dissertation (pp. 527-528 per Lim for the reconstruction).

new_statements.rule_in_words: In disyllabic non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, numerals) stress falls on the second syllable; disyllabic verbs are never stressed on the second syllable and (on limited data) carry first-syllable stress. Stress is a non-contrastive prosodic feature cued mainly by higher pitch; Amdo has no lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs: σ1, not σ2 (Caplow 2016 abstract, 'limited data'). Conflicting first-hand description for one migrant variety: Suzuki & Sonam Wangmo 2016: 105 (Shingnyag Tibetan, Lhagang) report stress 'on the first syllable of a polysyllabic word' as an often-prominent, non-distinctive prosodic feature. Suzuki 2017 (SAG7: 42) says it is not yet clear whether Amdo stress is distinctive or merely prosodic. Ebihara 2024: 6 (Gonghe nomad dialect) gives as an example pitch pattern 'first syllable low, second and later syllables high', non-distinctive, which is consistent with σ2 prominence in non-verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, disyllabic words in citation form; Caplow's abstract does not state the domain for longer words or phrases. All opened sources agree Amdo Tibetan is non-tonal (Makley et al. 1999: 112; Ebihara 2010: 43; Suzuki 2017 Table 1; Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 sec. 9.5.6) and that stress is not phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (Caplow 2016) describes Rebkong (Reb gong / Tongren, Qinghai) Amdo, a core Kokonor-area variety within amdo1237 (no separate Glottolog code seen). The corroborating pedagogical description (Ebihara 2024) is the Gonghe County (Gyai village) nomad dialect, also amdo1237. The one conflicting first-hand statement (Suzuki & Sonam Wangmo 2016: first-syllable prominence) is for Shingnyag Tibetan, an Amdo-type migrant variety spoken in Lhagang, Kangding (Khams Minyag), also without its own Glottolog code.

sources.quote: Given that the stress pattern of disyllables (except compound verbs) was iambic in Old Tibetan and remained this way all along down to modern Amdo dialects (Caplow, 2009), these irregular reflexes can be explained by a stress-induced lengthening in a period preceding Mid-Long-Raising: CA *ɑ < *aː lengthened from OT a, CA *u < *uː <Mid-Long-Raising *oː lengthened from OT o.
sources.locator: footnote 26, author's-draft p. 30; published version Bulletin of SOAS 79(2): 347-374
sources.note: Second-hand: the stress statement is attributed to Caplow 2009 (the author's UCSB dissertation), not Gong's own data. Iambic stress on disyllables with (compound) verbs excepted matches the catalog's rule for amdo1237 (sigma-2 on disyllabic non-verbs, verbs not on sigma-2, from Caplow 2016). Used by Gong only to explain irregular second-syllable vowel reflexes (Mdo.la rdzə.ma 'eyelash', Them.chen -pu ~ -wu < OT po ~ bo) as stress-induced lengthening. sources.citation: Zhou, Qian, Yonghong Li & Lei Guo. 2020. An Acoustic Study of English Word Stress of Amdo English Learners. Theory and Practice in Language Studies 10(1): 117-122. doi:10.17507/tpls.1001.17
sources.quote: most of the previous and present studies showed that for each individual Amdo word, there is no especially strongly articulated syllable or syllables, which means no syllable is stressed in sigle Amdo word. In phonetics, we name this phenomenon as “Amdo language doesn’t have word stress” (Duan Haifeng, 2012, p56). But still some researchers tried to prove that Amdo does have word stress (Shuangchen Wang,2012), but the evidences are not enough [...] So, at this stage of this study Amdo is taken as has no word stress. [...] if we reverse the inference, about this finding, we can get that Amdo words should have word stress and the position of the stress are quite likely not on the beginning of the words.

sources.note: This work describes Shar Tibetan (Sharwa / Sharkhog group, Shar-smad subgroup), Astong [Dazhai, A-stong] dialect, Dazhai Township, Songpan County, Aba Prefecture, Sichuan. The work never mentions Rebkong / Reb-gong / 熱貢 / 同仁 and contains no description of any Amdo Tibetan variety. It states (p. 118-119) that Shar Tibetan and Amdo Tibetan speakers are basically mutually unintelligible, so its register description cannot be transferred to Rebkong Amdo. Nothing usable for the amdo1237 entry (classification morphological, no-tone).

Word by word, pitch patterns like the Japanese accent are observed, for example pronouncing the first syllable low and the second and following syllables high, but these have no meaning-distinguishing function.' Confirms the catalog tone class no-tone. Silent on stress: no section on accent/stress; the pronunciation part (pp. 5-23) covers only syllable structure, vowels and consonants, and the appendix (pp. 198-203) is a verb-conjugation table

tone.quote: ■声調はない アムド・チベット語は多くの他のチベット語と違い，音程や旋律線の違い (声調) によって単語の意味の区別を行いません。単語ごとに，たとえば最初の音節を低く，2 音節目以降を高く発音するなど，日本語のアクセントのような音の高低パターンがみられますが，これらには意味を弁別する機能はありません。

sources.quote: In Zhangla, the low register correlates directly with rhyme length at the phonetic level, such that monosyllables containing long rhymes tend to be realised in a redundant low (phonetically low rising) tone, especially when the onset is voiced or voiceless aspirated
sources.locator: p. 41 (§2.2.1, fn 14); Amdo atonal stage p. 37 (§2)
sources.note: First-hand ('Personal research', fn 14). Subphonemic (allophonic) low register conditioned by rhyme length; no phonemic tone claimed. p. 37: Old Tibetan atonal stage 'still attested in some varieties of Amdo Tibetan', where non-suffix syllables are generally high-registered. No amdo1237 record; nothing on stress.
